content:
Quick answer: Many people with arthritis say their joints feel stiffer and more painful in cold, damp UK weather, though research on exactly why is mixed. Keep your home and joints warm, keep moving indoors on bad days, use warmth for stiffness, and check GOV.UK for winter heating help. See your GP if a joint becomes hot and swollen or pain is much worse than usual.

As the clocks go back, many of the people we hear from say their knees, hips and hands start to complain. Whether it is the cold, damp, changes in air pressure or simply moving less, winter can make arthritis harder. Studies disagree about how much weather itself changes joint pain, but your experience is real and there is plenty you can do. This guide covers keeping warm, keeping moving and getting help with heating costs.

Why winter can feel worse

  • Cold muscles and joints feel stiffer and less flexible
  • Moving less — dark evenings and icy paths mean fewer walks, and joints stiffen with stillness
  • Weather changes — some people notice pain before rain or cold snaps; the research is mixed
  • Less daylight — mood and sleep can dip, which makes pain feel louder
  • Cold homes — the NHS advises keeping rooms you use warm, especially if you are older or have a long-term condition

Keep yourself and your joints warm

  • Heat the rooms you use most to a comfortable temperature — NHS guidance suggests at least 18°C if you can
  • Layers, gloves, thermal socks and knee warmers trap heat better than one thick jumper
  • A warm shower or wheat bag eases morning stiffness; wrap a cold pack instead if a joint is hot and swollen. See the flare-up guide for the difference
  • Warm drinks and regular meals help keep your body warm

Keep moving when it is cold and dark

  1. Indoor routines — 10 minutes of gentle exercises from the exercise hub, twice a day
  2. Walk when it is light and dry — supportive footwear helps; our walking guide shows how to build up
  3. Warm water — many leisure centres run warm-water or aquatic sessions that suit stiff joints
  4. Pace yourself — spread chores out so cold, stiff days do not turn into crashes; see pacing and energy management

Ice and snow raise the risk of falls. Use grips on shoes, keep a stick or rail on the icy side, and ask someone else to grit paths if you can. Our staying active in winter guide has more ideas.

Help with heating costs

Cold homes are bad for joints and general health. Check GOV.UK for the Winter Fuel Payment and Cold Weather Payment, and contact your energy supplier if you are struggling to pay. If arthritis limits your daily living, the Benefits & PIP hub explains PIP, and if you are over State Pension age, read our Attendance Allowance guide. Extra income can make heating more affordable.

Vitamin D in winter

From October to March, UK sunlight is too weak to make enough vitamin D. The NHS advises everyone to consider a daily 10 microgram supplement during these months, and some people all year round. It supports bone and muscle health; it is not a treatment for arthritis pain itself.

When to see your GP

  • A joint becomes hot, red and swollen, especially with fever
  • Pain is much worse than your usual winter pattern or wakes you every night
  • Fingers or toes turn white or blue in the cold and are painful (possible Raynaud's)
  • Low mood is building as the days shorten

Pair practical winter steps with our pain relief guide and sleeping with arthritis guide for long, dark nights.

Frequently asked questions

Can weather really affect arthritis?

Many people say so, and some studies find a small link while others do not. Either way, keeping warm and moving tends to help.

Should I move somewhere warmer?

Some people feel better in warm, dry climates, but there is no guarantee and arthritis continues wherever you live. Focus first on warmth and activity at home.

Heat or cold for winter stiffness?

Warmth usually suits stiff, achy joints. Use a wrapped cold pack for a hot, swollen joint.
